title: How Subtext Works In Practice
use_cases: Use when developing authentic character interactions that avoid 'on-the-nose' dialogue
Implement when creating narrative tension between competing characters
Configure when showing emotional truth through actions rather than direct statements
Use when illustrating shifts in power dynamics or status between peers
content:
Two coworkers. One just got the promotion the other wanted.

No subtext (boring): “Congratulations on the promotion. I wanted it, but you deserved it more.” “Thanks. I know you wanted it too. I hope this doesn’t hurt our friendship.”

With subtext (alive): “So. Corner office.” “It’s not that big.” “No, it’s great. Really. You’ll do great.” “We should grab lunch sometime. Catch up.” “Sure. Yeah. Let me know when you’re free.”

Neither character says what they feel. The passed-over coworker performs graciousness badly. The promoted one tries to minimize and reconnect but knows the relationship just changed. Readers feel the tension in what’s not said.
